newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Outlying Jewish settlement grows under Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Outlying Jewish settlement grows under Netanyahu.

text.p: The leader of this Jewish settlement deep in the Israeli-occupied West Bank says his community is growing under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud-led government.

"It's no secret the government changed in June 1996. Bibi did not hide his intentions," Dov Odeser, 34, mayor of the hilltop settlement that offers a bird's-eye view of surrounding Arab villages, said this week, using Netanyahu's nickname.
Eli, near the self-ruled Palestinian town of Nablus, is a microcosm of settlement activity renewed under Netanyahu.

The Labour-led government he ousted in elections last May had frozen the building and sale of housing units at settlements deep in the West Bank, in areas it apparently did not intend to try to hold on to in a final peace deal with the Palestinians.

Some 3,000 housing units were affected. At Eli, 300 homes just built or under construction were frozen. Netanyahu's government lifted the edict and Odeser said 150 homes have been sold in the last two months.
Odeser said prices start at $39,000 for a tiny bungalow on a small plot of land. In central Israel, prices for single family homes begin at about $250,000.
For now, there is little new building at Eli, home to 300 families, or in other settlements deep in the West Bank.

The government will not give figures on how much construction is going on, but Israel's Peace Now group which monitors settlement, estimates about 4,000 home starts have been approved since Netanyahu took power.

Many of the new homes, as was the case under the last government, are in communities along the pre-1967 Middle East war border. Half-built homes have to be completed and sold before further building at places like Eli, Odeser said.
Yechiel Leiter, spokesman for the YESHA settler council, lives in Eli. He pointed to a row of roofless homes that had obviously been standing half-built for years.
"It's a whole mess (caused by the freeze)...but there's no impediment to build now," he said.

The only new settlement begun under Netanyahu is in Arab East Jerusalem. The 6,500-unit project, started in March, plunged Israel-Palestinian relations into crisis and touched off the current wave of violence in the West Bank.

Netanyahu's government pushed the Jerusalem settlement to emphasise it would not cede any part of the holy city, whose future status is to be negotiated in talks with the PLO on a permanent peace accord.

Netanyahu vowed on Thursday ahead of a meeting next week with U.S. President Bill Clinton not to relinquish what he called a right to settle Jews in lands captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
More than 130,000 Jews have settled amidst nearly two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza since 1967.

Leiter, looking out over steep West Bank hills sprinkled with blood-red poppies, said Palestinians could keep self-rule enclaves set up under interim peace deals, but the rest of the land would go to Jewish settlement, not a Palestinian state.
"Two things more or less have been settled...We are going to settle the land. We're not going to rule over the Arabs...I think that Netanyahu is ideologically onboard," Leiter said.
